title: A Good Walk Ruined: The History of Golf
summary: Josh and Chuck (labeled "iHeart Intro" in this transcript) discuss the history of golf, prompted by a researched piece by writer Livia. Topics cover disputed origins (Dutch word "colf", Scotland as the birthplace), early Scottish bans by James II and later lifting of the ban by James IV, Mary Queen of Scots, early courses like St. Andrews and the Open, the 13 Articles and the Honorable Company of Edinburgh Golfers, golf's spread to England and the U.S., Charles Blair McDonald and the origin of the USGA, changes in club and ball technology, caddies, golf magazines and cartoons, and the history of race and gender in the sport, including early Black and women's golf associations. The episode also includes a long host segment promoting the new podcast Three Putt Bogey, hosted by the chatting host with Adam Pranica, and some off-topic banter about racquetball and Happy Gilmore.

segments.title: Opening banter and golf fandom
segments.summary: The hosts chat about Chuck's golf hobby and his new podcast, and joke about the golf history episode ahead.

segments.title: Promotion for Three Putt Bogey
segments.summary: Chuck promotes his new golf podcast Three Putt Bogey with Adam Pranica, released September 25, and its social media.

segments.title: Golf stats and Caddyshack quote
segments.summary: Chuck cites golf's economic and participation statistics and a Caddyshack line; the hosts discuss Happy Gilmore and a Will Ferrell golf show.

segments.title: Origins of the word golf
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Dutch origin of the word golf (kolf), spelling variants, and early golf-like games, and describe what early golf looked like in 16th-century Scotland.

segments.title: Short golf, long golf and royal bans
segments.summary: Short golf played in town streets and long golf played on open land are distinguished. A 1457 act of parliament under James II banned golf, and Sunday sticks were used to sneak in play; later bans in 1471 and 1491 followed.

segments.title: Links, fairway and the ban lifted
segments.summary: Links land and the fairway term are explained. In 1502 James IV lifted the ban after taking up golf, and Mary, Queen of Scots, is described as playing golf and facing smears for it.

segments.title: Early golf records and St Andrews
segments.summary: Surviving documents are reviewed, including a 1743 poem The Golf, Thomas Kincaid's 1687 diary, and an 1857 instruction book. St Andrews' Old Course is described as the oldest surviving course, with a 1552 charter by John Hamilton.

segments.title: The Open and the Royal and Ancient Golf Club
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the name the Open versus British Open, the 1552 charter, the 18-hole standard, and the Royal and Ancient Golf Club's role as rules authority and manager of the Open.

segments.title: Masters tickets banter
segments.summary: Light banter about the Masters in Augusta and the hosts' roles as color commentators.

segments.title: 13 Articles and golf in England
segments.summary: The 13 Articles of the Honorable Company of Edinburgh Golfers (1744) and the Silver Club are described. James I brought golf to England, a course was built at Blackheath, and golf spread in England after doctors and Scottish professionals brought it back.

segments.title: Golf courses in England and farmer opposition
segments.summary: Courses in England often closed quickly, and the hosts compare this to racquetball clubs. Early English courses were mostly nine holes; the spread displaced cattle grazing and angered farmers.

segments.title: Class and the Industrial Revolution
segments.summary: Golf was an upper-class pursuit that the rising industrial middle class adopted. The railroad made it easier to reach the shires.

segments.title: Transition
segments.summary: Brief banter about letting frustration go before moving to U.S. history.

segments.title: Early golf in the United States
segments.summary: Golf in the American colonies dates to 1659 in Fort Orange (Albany), where Dutch authorities banned street golf over windows. David Dees brought gear to Charleston; Harleston Green (1841) was an early club where enslaved people worked as caddies. St Andrews in Yonkers (1888) is noted as a long-running U.S. course; Canada's Royal Montreal Club (1873) is noted as older.

segments.title: Charles Blair McDonald and the USGA
segments.summary: Charles Blair McDonald, a Chicago golf architect who studied at St Andrews, lost two tournaments in a row and angered the field by alleging cheating. Clubs including St Andrews formed a rules body that became the USGA.

segments.title: Golf club technology history
segments.summary: Early clubs were hand-made wood; names like play club, brassy, spoon, cleek, baffy, and Nick Blick are explained. Archibald Barry is credited with a standard set of irons, Spalding numbered irons in 1930, and metal woods came in the 1980s. The hosts discuss the Gutta percha ball replacing feather balls.

segments.title: Equipment R&D and optimization
segments.summary: The hosts discuss modern golf equipment research and the broader idea of optimization in everyday life.

segments.title: Caddies and golf professionals
segments.summary: The term caddy is described as a Scottish errand boy term. Caddies carried clubs and found balls, and were often teenagers or working-class adults in 19th-century England. Reformers pushed for better caddy treatment. Golf pros and clubs with Scottish professionals are described.

segments.title: Golf pros and staff
segments.summary: Hosts discuss pros on staff at clubs and the continuing tradition of club pros.

segments.title: Golf magazines, cartoons, and antique golf ads
segments.summary: Golf fever grew in the late 19th century with golf magazines and mentions in other publications. The hosts describe 19th-century Punch cartoons on head-lifting, and a novelty head-down device.

segments.title: Race, gender and golf access
segments.summary: Golf was long an elite white male pastime. Women's and African-American golf organizations formed in response, including the LPGA (1950), Chicago Women's Golf Club (1937), and the United Golfers Association (1925). Chuck discusses clubs still restricting access and golf becoming more democratic.

segments.title: Podcast plugs and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck promotes Three Putt Bogey and a cruise; the hosts joke about accounting and sign off with email info and iHeartRadio credits.
